title: Cold smoking cured pork
subtitle: Adding smoke flavour and further preserving a cured joint at low temperature.
excerpt: Cold smoking applies smoke at temperatures below 30 degrees Celsius, which adds flavour and deposits preservative compounds without cooking the meat. It is a finishing step applied after curing, not a substitute for it. Cold smoked bacon, ham, and loin develop a deeper, more complex flavour and a longer shelf life than their unsmoked equivalents. A cold smoker can be made very simply at home and run on hardwood sawdust or chips.
sourceNotes: Michael Ruhlman and Brian Polcyn, Charcuterie (2005), W. W. Norton. Gary Wittels and Ianna Hawkins Owen, The Smokehouse Cookbook (2021). Tim Hayward, The DIY Cook (2018), section on building a cold smoker. UK Food Standards Agency, smoked food guidance (2023). Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, The River Cottage Meat Book (2004).

glossaryTerms.definition: A process that exposes cured food to smoke at a temperature typically between 15 and 30 degrees Celsius, well below the temperature at which proteins denature or fat renders. Cold smoking flavours and partially preserves but does not cook.
A tray or maze-shaped trough filled with compressed sawdust pellets that burn slowly and generate cool smoke without significant heat. The most practical way to generate cold smoke for home use.

content.text: is always a secondary step: the meat must be fully cured before it enters the smoker. Smoke does not preserve uncured meat safely. Applied correctly to a cured piece, bacon, ham, or loin, cold smoke adds colour (a mahogany surface), flavour compounds from the combustion of wood sugars, and phenolic compounds that slow fat rancidity and surface mould.
Any enclosed chamber with a rack or hook for hanging meat and a way to introduce cool smoke can be used for cold smoking. Practical options:
An old refrigerator cabinet with the compressor removed. Drill a hole for the smoke inlet and a vent at the top.
A timber-built smoker box with a separate fire box connected by metal pipe. The pipe should be at least 1 m long so the smoke cools before reaching the meat.
A kettle barbecue or dedicated barrel smoker with a
inside, with the lid on. Run it in winter when ambient temperature naturally keeps the chamber below 25 degrees.
Hardwoods only: oak, beech, apple, cherry, alder, hickory. Each gives a different flavour profile; oak and beech are the traditional choices for British-style cured pork.
Never use softwoods (pine, spruce, cedar). They produce resinous smoke with compounds that taint flavour and are harmful to health.

Remove the cured meat from the refrigerator and allow it to come to the ambient temperature of the smoker space for one hour, surface-dry. A tacky or damp surface accepts smoke well; a wet surface can give a bitter, acrid smoke deposit.
Load the smoke generator and ignite one end. A maze-type generator filled with fine hardwood sawdust will burn for 8 to 12 hours producing a thin, continuous stream of cool smoke.
Place the meat in the chamber, with at least 50 mm clearance around each piece for smoke circulation.
Monitor the chamber temperature: it must not exceed 30 degrees Celsius. On a cold day in winter (5 to 10 degrees ambient), this manages itself. Above 15 degrees ambient, it requires management.
A single 8-hour session gives a mild smoke flavour. Traditional recipes call for multiple sessions of 8 to 12 hours over two to four days, with the meat returned to the refrigerator between sessions.

Cold smoking pork in UK summer is not practical without refrigeration in the smoke chamber: ambient air temperatures push the chamber well above the 30 degree threshold. Cold smoking is naturally a winter activity, which is why it historically paired with pig-killing season in November and December.

attrs.cue: Smoke flavour is harsh and bitter
attrs.cause: Meat surface was wet when smoking started, or smouldering fire producing thick black smoke rather than thin blue smoke
attrs.fix: Thin blue smoke is ideal. Thick, white or black smoke indicates the fire is producing soot and tars rather than smoke compounds. Ensure the pellet generator smoulders rather than flames. Dry the meat surface thoroughly before the next session.

attrs.cue: Pellet smoke generator keeps going out
attrs.cause: Draught in the chamber extinguishing the smoulder, or pellets damp
attrs.fix: Store sawdust and pellets in a dry place for at least two weeks before use. Block draughts in the chamber. The smoulder needs a small air inlet but not wind.
